newsitem.title: INDIA: Monsoon, low prices to spur Indian gold imports.
newsitem.headline: Monsoon, low prices to spur Indian gold imports.

text.p: India's gold imports are expected to rise sharply this year as farmers, anticipating a bountiful harvest after generous monsoon rains, take advantage of low world prices, trade officials said on Tuesday.
"Gold imports will cross 500 tonnes this calendar year," Makhan Lal Damani, president of the Bombay Bullion Association, told Reuters. India imported 409 tonnes of gold in 1996.
Damani said gold was currently quoted at 4,520 rupees ($126) per 10 grams compared with 5,180 rupees the same time last year.
"Now people are able to buy 15 percent more gold with the same price compared to what they were getting last year," he said.
Rajiv Damani of Damani Jewellers, a leading New Delhi gold trader, said substantial sales by large firms had pushed down world prices.
"The main selling is by the Australian and German banks," said Vinay Mehra of Dunroll Industries, another gold trader in the Indian capital.

India is the world's largest consumer of gold, although nearly a third of its 960 million people live below the poverty line. Per capita gross national product was $340 in 1995, according to the World Bank.
The country's annual gold consumption is estimated at more than 500 tonnes, most of it imported.
India's main demand is for gold jewellery, given and used each year at an estimated 10 million weddings and which absorbs nearly 300 tonnes of the metal annually, bullion dealers said.
Traders said the start of the Indian marriage season from September might push up domestic gold prices.
"The prices are lower currently but domestic prices might rise in the next few months," Rajiv Damani said.
Makhan Lal Damani added: "The current demand from the rural sector is very good as farmers have a lot of money after good crop harvests."
India harvested a record 198 million tonnes of grain in 1996/97 (July-June), up sharply from 185 million tonnes the previous year.

"The demand will further pick up on expectations of a good monsoon." On Monday the India Meteorological Department (IMD) said this year's monsoon, about half way over, has dropped normal to excess rainfall over 80 percent of the country.
Good monsoon rains generally boost farmers' incomes by raising agricultural output.
Last week, senior Reserve Bank of India (RBI) officials urged the government to allow free gold exports and imports to help boost industrial and employment growth and maintain a stable exchange rate.
Mehra said that allowing free imports of gold would help bring Indian prices in line with international prices and check smuggling.
"Although savings would be reduced if free imports are allowed, it will help curb smuggling," Mehra said.

Commerce Ministry officials say gold smuggling currently accounts for about 100 to 120 tonnes annually. It has come down from 250 tonnes since 1992 when India allowed non-resident Indians to bring in gold subject to duty. ($1=35.7 rupees)
